title: The Unpronounceable Professor reveals a Mimble Wimble Secret
description:
The foundation of Litecoin's MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks) is a unique type of encryption. This magic math gives LTC users the option to use MWEB for added privacy. 

Litecoin’s MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Block) is a powerful privacy and scalability upgrade that brings optional confidential transactions to the Litecoin network—while staying fully compatible with existing Litecoin wallets and exchanges.

MWEB allows users to send private Litecoin (LTC) transactions by hiding transaction amounts and reducing on-chain data. Unlike privacy coins that enforce anonymity by default, Litecoin’s MWEB is opt-in, giving users the freedom to choose between transparent transactions or enhanced privacy when they need it.

🔐 What MWEB Does for Litecoin

Improves Privacy: Transaction amounts are hidden using MimbleWimble cryptography

Enhances Fungibility: All LTC remains interchangeable, supporting sound money principles

Boosts Scalability: Transaction data is compressed, reducing blockchain bloat

Maintains Compliance: Core Litecoin transactions remain transparent and unchanged

Fully Optional: Users can move LTC in and out of MWEB at any time

⚙️ How MWEB Works

MWEB runs as an extension block, meaning it operates alongside Litecoin’s main blockchain without altering its base layer. This innovative design keeps Litecoin secure, decentralized, and accessible—while adding modern privacy features.

🚀 Why MWEB Matters

MWEB positions Litecoin as digital silver—fast, low-fee, and now more private. It strengthens Litecoin’s role as sound money, ideal for everyday payments, peer-to-peer transfers, and long-term value storage.

asr.full_text: PAPA popcorn because this is the Big Brain episode and because you have a big brain I will explain it to you in a way that you will love it. 5. The foundation of M Web is encryption and encryption simply means transforming a dataset for example a transaction amount with a key so that the result is unrecognizable to anybody who doesn't have that key. Nambo Wimbo is a unique type of encryption that allows the protocol to be able to perform additions on encrypted amounts without revealing what is inside. How does it do this? That's where the secret Mass Magic comes in play. This is the formula and I know it might look complicated but I will break it down for you using a simple example. This part of the equation on the left represents coins being sent and this part of the equation on the right represents coins being received and this part of the equation on the right represent for example coins being received. Amount is the coin itself and key is the encryption key of the coin so you can think about it more like gold coins and paper used to wrap the gold coin so that nobody can see that it is there. The sum total of the figures on the left must balance the sum total of the figures of the Right. But how can Membo Wemble calculate the values on both sides when the amounts are encrypted? It uses a kernel! Now a kernel is a zero value coin that has its own encryption. So you can think about it like wrapped paper but without any coins inside. This kernel is added to one side of the equation to balance things out and it does this because the encryption key to the kernel is the difference between both sides of the equation. And just like that, it balances out. Now, here are some important things to note. 1 The protocol only validates a transaction, if the Creator knows the keys to the coins they want to spend. 2 They must prove it without revealing the encryption key itself. 3 MemboWembo requires the kernel to be signed with its own private key and that signature proves that the kernel is in fact a zero value coin that is neither creating nor destroying the value. The transaction creator knows the kernel key and since the key is the difference between both sides of the equation, it indirectly proves that all input and output in fact exist without revealing any of them. Now that is the magic that Nmimbo Wenbo uses to keep transactions hidden while proving that they are in fact valid. This presentation was done by Hector Chou so credits to him. That's it from me today, as usual I am your professor Nkutwe Nketu Nkete Mbakwe and I will see you in the next episode.
